title: Welded Wire Mesh Specifications: What to Include
description: Learn which welded wire mesh specifications to include in an RFQ or submittal, from wire size and spacing to openings, finish, format, and documentation.
html:
A complete welded wire mesh specification should identify the application, material and coating, wire size or area designation, longitudinal and transverse spacing, resulting opening, sheet or roll dimensions, tolerances, weld or mechanical performance, packaging, and required documentation. Gauge, wire diameter, and an area designation are not interchangeable. The fastest way to review a submittal is to decode each field against the current drawing and specification, not to approve a familiar-looking mesh label.

Start With the Application and the Required Function

Start by identifying the function stated in the drawings or specification, then use that function to interpret the mesh notation and review the supplier’s submittal. The same phrase, “welded wire mesh,” can describe a reinforcement product, a framing-related infill, welded wire lath, or a security product. Those categories use different terminology and performance criteria.

Write the function in plain language before reviewing a designation. The requirement might be concrete reinforcement, non-structural infill behind an interior finish, a plaster or stucco base, or a barrier that must resist access. A submittal that names only a mesh opening does not identify enough information for technical approval.

Also identify whether the mesh is part of a designed assembly or a general fabrication item. Structural reinforcement needs design-controlled properties and placement information. An interior framing-related submittal may depend more heavily on stud spacing, attachment, clearances, openings, and coordination with board or finish materials.

Separate Reinforcing Mesh From Interior Framing and Other Mesh Categories

Do not transfer a specification from one mesh category to another. Concrete reinforcement, interior framing-related mesh, welded wire lath, and security mesh can use different terminology and performance criteria, so the application must control how the submittal is decoded and checked.

ApplicationSpecifications that usually control the reviewDetails that require project confirmation
Concrete reinforcementWire size or area designation, longitudinal and transverse spacing, steel properties, sheet or roll form, laps, supports, placement, and required standardsDesign drawings, structural notes, cover, lap or splice requirements, placement tolerances, and engineer-approved documentation
Interior framing-related workOpening, wire diameter, spacing in both directions, attachment method, edge condition, clearances, corrosion exposure, and compatibility with the framing assemblyStud layout, service penetrations, movement zones, finish system, fire or acoustic assembly, and approved installation detail
Welded wire lathForm, coating, sheet or roll dimensions, attachment, overlap, and compatibility with the specified plaster or render systemFinish manufacturer requirements, substrate, exposure, fasteners, joints, corners, and project standard
Security meshOpening, wire diameter, panel dimensions, edge treatment, frame connection, finish, and resistance requirementsSecurity level, test method, frame design, access requirements, corrosion exposure, and owner requirements

Ontario Regulation 275/11 identifies fabricating, handling, sorting, cutting, bending, rigging, placing, welding, and tying welded wire mesh used to reinforce concrete constructions within the reinforcing-rodworker scope of practice. The same regulation distinguishes interior framing and wall-system installation from those reinforcing-concrete provisions. It does not approve a particular product, design, or application. Read the Ontario scope provision for welded wire mesh reinforcement and the separate interior framing and wall-system provision for the regulatory distinction.

How to Read a Welded Wire Mesh Designation

A mesh designation normally communicates the wire size, spacing in each direction, product style, and supplied dimensions. Some systems use wire diameter or gauge, while welded wire reinforcement commonly uses an area-based designation. Read the notation according to the system that created it instead of converting terms by assumption.

Wire size, gauge, and area designation

Wire diameter is a physical measurement stated in millimetres, inches, or another specified unit. Gauge is a size label, not a universal substitute for diameter. Gauge systems and naming conventions can vary, so a submittal should identify the governing system and, where relevant, the actual diameter.

W/M or area designation expresses steel area per unit length in a direction. It is not the same thing as gauge or diameter. Require the supplier to state the underlying wire information used in the designation.

Longitudinal spacing, transverse spacing, and opening

Longitudinal and transverse spacing describe the center-to-center distance between wires in two directions. Clear opening is related to spacing and wire diameter, but it should be verified from the product drawing or data sheet because edge geometry, manufacturing tolerances, and measurement direction affect the result.

For a simple illustrative grid with equal wires and regular spacing, a nominal clear opening is approximately the center spacing minus the wire diameter. That relationship explains the geometry, but it does not replace the stated product opening or project requirement.

Annotated illustrative designation

Consider this clearly hypothetical notation: 6 mm wire at 100 mm by 150 mm spacing, flat sheet, 1,200 mm by 2,400 mm. It identifies the wire diameter, the two center spacings, the flat-sheet format, and the nominal sheet dimensions.

This example does not establish structural capacity, code compliance, coating, weld strength, tolerance, or suitability. A complete submittal would still state the material, finish, edge condition, quantity, packaging, documentation, and project-specific performance requirements.

Decode the Specification Fields Before Approving the Submittal

A reviewable specification gives the supplier enough information to identify one product and gives the project team enough information to compare that product with the contract documents. Use these fields as the minimum framework for an RFQ or submittal review.

  • Application and function: State whether the mesh is for reinforcement, framing-related work, lath, security, fabrication, or another purpose.
  • Base material: Identify the material required by the drawings, specification, or exposure condition.
  • Coating or finish: State whether the project requires galvanized, coated, stainless, painted, or uncoated material. “Galvanized” alone does not prove suitability for every exposure.
  • Wire size: Give diameter, gauge with its governing system, or area designation. Ask for the corresponding physical wire information.
  • Spacing: State longitudinal and transverse spacing separately.
  • Opening: Identify whether the required dimension is clear opening, nominal opening, or center spacing, and state the measurement direction.
  • Product style: Specify flat sheets, rolls, welded panels, bent panels, or another approved form.
  • Dimensions: State sheet or roll width, length, allowable variation, and any cut, bend, or custom dimensions.
  • Edges and ends: Identify overhang, trimmed edges, selvage, projecting wires, or a finished perimeter.
  • Performance: List yield strength, elongation, weld shear strength, load capacity, or other properties only when project documents establish them.
  • Tolerances: Include dimensional, spacing, wire diameter, flatness, coating, and weld tolerances when they control fit or compliance.
  • Quantity and packaging: State the number of sheets or rolls, estimated area, bundle requirements, labels, and handling protection.
  • Documentation: Request drawings, data sheets, material certificates, coating information, test reports, certificates of conformance, and installation instructions where required.

During review, mark each field as confirmed, not applicable, or unresolved. A generic catalogue table can explain available configurations, but it does not prove that the submitted mesh meets the project’s design, coating, tolerance, or documentation requirements.

Review Sheets and Rolls Against the Installation Detail

The sheet or roll format is a submittal field, not a standalone quality decision. Check the proposed format against the approved installation method, panel dimensions, access, seams, openings, storage, and handling conditions shown or described in the project documents.

Flat sheets generally provide controlled panel dimensions, predictable edges, and rigid placement. They also create seams and can produce more offcuts around irregular openings.

Rolls provide a flexible format that may suit approved long runs, but the submittal should address unrolling space, temporary control, cutting, straightening, storage, overlaps, and seams. A roll is not an automatic substitute for a sheet-controlled detail.

Review conditionQuestions for a sheet submittalQuestions for a roll submittal
AccessCan the proposed panels be carried and positioned in the available space?Is there room to unroll and control the material without distortion?
GeometryDo panel edges, openings, and repeated modules match the layout?Is flexible placement approved for the required geometry?
Seams and wasteWhere are panel joints and cut edges located?How are overlaps, seams, and cut lengths controlled?
Installation controlDoes the detail preserve flatness and alignment?What method holds alignment while unrolling and fastening?
StorageCan panels be stacked and labeled on a dry, stable surface?Will roll storage prevent distortion, damage, or uncontrolled movement?

Compare the proposed format with the installation detail instead of accepting a change based only on price per unit. Any change in cutting, overlaps, seams, supports, handling, access, waste, packaging, or placement method should be recorded as a submittal deviation.

Use Project Documents to Set Performance Requirements

Project documents should establish requirements affecting structural performance, life safety, durability, or formal compliance. The design professional, project specification, applicable standard, or approving authority may control steel strength, elongation, weld shear strength, coating mass, corrosion resistance, dimensional tolerance, laps, cover, attachment, or testing.

Ask the design team or project specification to identify the governing standard and acceptance criteria. Do not infer an ASTM, CSA, building-code, coating, or weld requirement from a general mesh chart. Certification or test evidence must correspond to the actual product, size, finish, and manufacturing condition being submitted.

For interior framing-related work, coordinate mesh with stud spacing, fasteners, board or finish layers, service penetrations, movement joints, head-of-wall conditions, and required clearances. A product that fits the nominal opening may still interfere with an attachment or movement detail.

For concrete reinforcement, placement drawings and structural design control wire position, cover, laps, supports, openings, and continuity. The Ontario scope regulation identifies welded wire mesh in the context of reinforcing concrete, but it does not establish design values or approve a particular product.

Worked Example: Turn a Requirement Into a Reviewable RFQ

The following is a hypothetical document-review example, not a universal design or product recommendation. It shows how incomplete language can become a request that a supplier can price and a project team can review.

Starting requirement

A contractor receives a requirement for mesh in a non-structural interior assembly. The drawings identify a regular grid, flat installation, and required clearance around service openings. The project team has not yet documented material, finish, tolerance, or supporting product data.

Convert it into an RFQ

  • Application: Non-structural interior assembly, with drawing detail and revision identified.
  • Product form: Flat welded panels, subject to installation-detail approval.
  • Illustrative geometry: 6 mm wire at 100 mm by 150 mm center spacing. The project team must confirm whether this is the actual design requirement.
  • Dimensions: Panel width and length matched to the layout, with stated tolerance and allowance for the opening schedule.
  • Material and finish: Proposed against exposure and specification, not assumed from the word “mesh.”
  • Edges: Trimmed or projecting wires identified from attachment and clearance details.
  • Quantity: Panel count, estimated area, approved-cut allowance, and packaging requirements.
  • Documents: Product drawing, wire information, spacing and opening data, finish details, tolerances, weld information, certificates, and installation guidance.

Review the returned submittal

Compare every field against the request. If the submittal states only “6 mm mesh” but omits spacing directions, panel dimensions, finish, and edge condition, it is incomplete even if the wire diameter appears correct.

Check whether the stated opening is clear opening or center-to-center spacing. Confirm that the product drawing matches the requested format and that certificates or test information apply to the submitted wire, finish, and manufacturing configuration. Record unresolved items as questions instead of filling them with assumptions.

RFQ and Submittal Checklist

Before requesting a price

  • Identify the intended application and required function.
  • Attach the current drawing, specification section, detail, and revision.
  • State whether the mesh is structural, non-structural, finish-related, security-related, or fabrication-related.
  • Define wire diameter, gauge system, or area designation.
  • State longitudinal and transverse spacing separately.
  • Define clear opening, nominal opening, or center spacing.
  • Specify material, coating, finish, edge condition, tolerances, and product form.
  • List dimensions, cut requirements, quantity, packaging, labels, and delivery constraints.
  • Identify required standards, certificates, test reports, drawings, and installation documents.
  • Flag values requiring design-professional or owner approval.

Before approving a submittal

  • Match the submitted product description to the RFQ and current drawings.
  • Confirm the wire information behind any gauge or area designation.
  • Check both spacing directions and the opening definition.
  • Verify dimensions, quantity, edges, tolerances, and packaging.
  • Review material and coating evidence against project exposure.
  • Confirm weld and mechanical performance documents apply to the submitted configuration.
  • Coordinate openings, attachments, overlaps, seams, clearances, and movement zones.
  • Resolve deviations in writing before release, fabrication, or installation.

Common Specification Mistakes That Create Rework

Naming only the opening

“25 mm mesh” does not identify wire diameter, spacing, material, finish, format, or tolerance. State what the number measures and add wire information and both spacing directions.

Mixing gauge, diameter, and area

A gauge label, measured diameter, and area designation describe different kinds of information. Require the supplier to show the relationship between shorthand and physical product.

Omitting transverse spacing

A product with 100 mm spacing in both directions is not the same as one with 100 mm by 150 mm spacing. The second direction affects openings, wire quantity, fit, and assembly coordination.

Assuming galvanized means suitable everywhere

Galvanizing can be relevant to corrosion resistance, but suitability depends on exposure, contact with other materials, finish requirements, and project specification. Confirm the required coating or finish through project documents.

Accepting a format change without reviewing the detail

A roll may create alignment, straightening, seam, storage, or opening problems where the detail expects controlled panels. Review the proposed format against the approved installation detail and record any deviation.

Ignoring openings and clearances

Mesh can conflict with penetrations, fasteners, framing edges, movement zones, or embedded components. Review the opening schedule and attachment detail before approving dimensions or cutting patterns.

Approving a catalogue table as compliance evidence

A reference table helps explain designations and compare options. It is not proof that the submitted product meets engineering, code, coating, tolerance, or testing requirements.

Prepare the Final Mesh Request

The strongest welded wire mesh request connects the project function to a decoded designation, then connects that designation to drawings, installation conditions, performance evidence, and delivery requirements. If a requirement is unknown, mark it as an approval question instead of allowing a supplier or installer to infer it.

Send the completed RFQ and the current supporting drawings to the responsible supplier and project team. Keep the approved designation, submittal response, unresolved questions, and final acceptance together in the project record.
